blocks.title: What the interviewer is really testing
blocks.text: This is **not a booking search problem**. Search is easy and cacheable. Check-in is a **fixed-inventory, high-contention write problem**: 300 seats, one flight, thousands of passengers hitting `CheckIn` in the same minute at T-24h. The interviewer wants to hear you say: **inventory cannot be oversold, concurrent seat picks must serialize, and reads must survive a write hotspot.** If you start with microservices and Kafka, you fail. If you start with the seat row lock, you pass.

Design the **airline check-in subsystem** for scheduled flights. Passengers with an existing `PNR / booking` check in between 24h and 1h before departure, pick or auto-get a seat, and receive a boarding pass. Inventory is fixed per aircraft layout — e.g. 180-380 seats — and immutable after schedule publish. The system must prevent **double-assignment of the same seat**, handle **concurrent check-ins for the same flight**, support **seat holds, seat changes, group seating, overbooked / standby handling, and un-check-in**, and stay available when one popular flight gets hammered while thousands of other flights are idle.

items: `GET /bookings/{pnr}` — fetch booking, passengers, flight, eligibility window.
`GET /flights/{id}/seatmap` — current seat availability, versioned per flight.
`POST /checkins {pnr, passengerIds, seatPreference?, idempotencyKey}` — check in one or more passengers.
`POST /checkins/{id}/seat {seatId, idempotencyKey}` — explicit seat pick or change.

blocks.text: Scale that matters: ~5,000 flights/day, ~1M check-ins/day average, but **burst is per-flight, not global**. A 300-seat A320 will see 200+ concurrent `POST /checkins` in the first 60 seconds after check-in opens, plus retries from mobile. Reads of the seat map are 50-100x writes. **Trade-off:** you optimize for single-flight write serialization and globally scalable reads — not for uniform QPS. Consistency beats availability on the seat row; availability beats consistency on the seat-map view.
Do not jump to architecture. Check-in has hidden business rules that change the database design completely. Ask in this order and lock answers on the whiteboard:

items.title: Booking vs check-in boundary?
items.text: Assume booking/PNR already exists? You do not build payment or pricing here. Check-in only consumes a valid booking. This cuts scope by half.

items.title: Assigned seating or first-come?
items.text: Can passengers pick exact seats, or auto-assign only? Exact pick means contended writes on hot seat rows (1A, exit rows). Auto-assign lets you pre-allocate blocks and avoid per-seat contention.

items.title: Overbooking and standby policy?
items.text: Is the flight allowed to check in 105% of seats and bump at gate? If yes, you need separate `capacity` vs `checkedInCount` and a standby queue — you cannot just do `seat.status = ASSIGNED`.

items.title: Idempotency and retries expected?
items.text: Mobile clients will retry POSTs. Agree that every mutating call carries an `Idempotency-Key`. Without it any lock design double-assigns on retry.

items.title: Seat change window and gate close?
items.text: Can seats change after check-in, after boarding-pass issue, after gate close? This defines your state machine and whether boarding-pass issue is just a read.

rows: Eligibility check: flight in window, booking valid, passenger not already checked in
Prevents 90% of invalid writes before touching hot seat rows
Decouples UX think-time from DB lock hold time
Exactly-once seat assignment per passenger, idempotent retries
Mobile retries must not create two boarding passes

Otherwise leaked HELD seats shrink a fixed cabin
No double-assign under 1000 concurrent picks on one flight
p99 check-in < 500ms, seatmap read < 100ms at burst
Writes serialize; reads must not queue behind them

Contention isolation is the scaling strategy

blocks.text: The naive design everyone proposes: one `seats` table, stateless service, `read seat row -> if AVAILABLE, UPDATE to ASSIGNED` in two round trips, plus a Redis cache of the seat map for speed. It looks clean and passes a single-threaded demo. It collapses the moment check-in opens because **read and write are not atomic** and the cache becomes the source of lies. Two passengers both read `12A=free` from cache, both issue UPDATE, last writer wins — or worse, both succeed. **Trade-off:** you bought low latency and simplicity and paid with lost updates and oversell. Fixed inventory has zero tolerance for that.

blocks.title: Exactly why it fails
blocks.text: Three fatal flaws: **1. No mutual exclusion** — the check and the update are separate statements, so concurrent transactions interleave. **2. Cache-write divergence** — you invalidate cache after DB write, so 500 readers see stale FREE for seconds. **3. Lock hold during user think time** — if you hold a DB transaction while the user stares at the seat map, connections exhaust and one flight takes down the pool. The fix is not a bigger DB. It is a different concurrency unit.

Partition everything by `flightId`. Route all writes for one flight to one logical writer: either a **Postgres partition / shard keyed by flightId** with row-level locks, or a **per-flight queue** in front of it. Reads come from replicas + versioned seat-map cache. Writes are **short atomic transactions**: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the exact seat row, or an optimistic `UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE' AND version=?`. Seat selection UX uses **ephemeral holds in Redis with TTL**, confirmed asynchronously to Postgres. **Trade-off:** you accept ~100-300ms serialized writes per flight to guarantee correctness, and you buy back perceived speed with holds and cached reads. Throughput per flight is intentionally limited — that is the point.

blocks.title: Check-in request path
blocks.caption: Writes serialize per flight; reads fan out to replicas.
blocks.code:
graph TD
  C[Client app] --> LB[API Gateway]
  LB --> CS[Check-in Service]
  CS --> ELIG[Eligibility check]
  ELIG --> R[(Redis holds TTL)]
  R --> P[(Postgres primary by flightId)]
  P --> RR[(Read replica seatmap)]
  CS --> K[Kafka outbox]
  K --> B[Boarding-pass worker]
  K --> N[Notification worker]

blocks.text: Why Postgres as system of record and not pure Redis or Cassandra? Because you need **ACID row atomicity on a single seat**. `SELECT FOR UPDATE` or conditional UPDATE gives you linearizable seat assignment without distributed locks. Redis is a **lease manager**, not inventory truth — it can evict, fail over, and lose a hold. Cassandra gives you scale but `LWT` at 1000 contenders per partition is slow and operationally painful. **Trade-off:** Postgres limits single-flight write QPS to hundreds/sec, which is fine because a flight only has 300 seats. You shard by flight to get global throughput. Never scale the contended unit; isolate it.

blocks.title: Core tables
blocks.caption: Seat is the contention point; CheckinRecord makes retries safe.
blocks.code:
classDiagram
  class Booking {
    String pnr
    String flightId
    String status
    int passengerCount
  }
  class Seat {
    String seatId
    String flightId
    String cabin
    String status
    int version
  }
  class Hold {
    String holdId
    String seatId
    String passengerId
    int expiresAt
  }
  class CheckinRecord {
    String checkinId
    String idempotencyKey
    String seatId
    String boardingPassId
  }
  Booking --> CheckinRecord : yields
  Seat --> Hold : held by
  Seat --> CheckinRecord : assigned to

-- Partition by flight_id. Keep seat rows narrow and hot.
CREATE TABLE seats (
  flight_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  seat_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  cabin TEXT NOT NULL, -- Y, Y+, J
  status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'AVAILABLE', -- AVAILABLE, HELD, ASSIGNED, BLOCKED
  passenger_id TEXT,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (flight_id, seat_id)
) PARTITION BY HASH (flight_id);

CREATE TABLE checkins (
  checkin_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  flight_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  pnr TEXT NOT NULL,
  passenger_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  seat_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  boarding_pass_id TEXT UNIQUE,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (flight_id, passenger_id) -- one seat per passenger
);

CREATE INDEX ON checkins (flight_id, seat_id);

# Hold path: no DB lock while user thinks. Redis lease + Lua atomic check.
# Trade-off: hold is best-effort UX; confirm in Postgres is truth.
import redis
r = redis.Redis()
HOLD_LUA = """
if redis.call('EXISTS', KEYS[1]) == 1 then return 0 end
redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'EX', ARGV[2])
return 1
"""
# key = f"hold:{flight_id}:{seat_id}", value = passenger_id, ttl 120s
def try_hold(flight_id, seat_id, passenger_id, ttl=120):
    ok = r.eval(HOLD_LUA, 1, f"hold:{flight_id}:{seat_id}", passenger_id, ttl)
    return bool(ok)  # False -> someone else holds it, pick another seat

blocks.caption: Cost is per-seat-row, not per-flight-scan.
rows: No lock; versioned cache, invalidate per flight
No DB load; TTL auto-releases orphans
Serializes only on same seatId; different seats parallel
Pre-allocate contiguous blocks per party to avoid full scan
Must delete hold key and bump seatmap version

blocks.text: The interviewer will push: *what if 1000 people click 12A at once?* Answer with two mechanisms. First, **pessimistic on explicit pick, optimistic on auto-assign**. Explicit pick does `SELECT FOR UPDATE` on that one seat row — 999 wait ~50ms each, one wins, rest get `409 SeatTaken` with a fresh seat map version. That is correct and fast enough because the lock scope is one row, not the flight. Auto-assign must not lock the whole cabin; use `UPDATE seats SET ... WHERE flight_id=? AND status='AVAILABLE' AND cabin=? LIMIT 1` or a pre-shuffled free-list per cabin. **Trade-off:** pessimistic gives clear errors but creates a lock queue on hot seats; optimistic gives higher throughput but more abort-retry. Use each where its pain is cheapest. Second, **never hold a DB transaction across a user or network call**. Hold in Redis, confirm in a <50ms DB transaction. Add a per-flight in-memory queue or rate limiter if the DB primary shows lock-wait spikes — shed load with fast failure, not longer queues.

blocks.title: Seat lifecycle
blocks.caption: Every exit releases inventory; TTL is the safety net.
blocks.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> AVAILABLE
  AVAILABLE --> HELD : hold TTL 120s
  HELD --> AVAILABLE : expire or release
  HELD --> ASSIGNED : confirm txn
  AVAILABLE --> ASSIGNED : auto-assign txn
  ASSIGNED --> AVAILABLE : uncheckin
  ASSIGNED --> BOARDED : gate scan
  BOARDED --> [*]

blocks.text: Boarding-pass generation and notifications must be **transactional outbox**, not inline. Inside the confirm transaction, write to an `outbox` table; a relay publishes to Kafka. The pass renderer is idempotent on `checkinId`. If it crashes, replay yields the same `boardingPassId`. **Trade-off:** you add ~seconds of eventual consistency to passes/notifications to keep the seat transaction tiny and infallible. Also cap overbooking explicitly: maintain `flights.checked_in_count` with a conditional increment `WHERE checked_in_count < max_allowed`, separate from seat assignment, so standby and bump logic cannot corrupt seat truth.

items.title: Group / family seating together?
items.text: Do not lock N rows in random order — deadlock. Sort seatIds, lock in order, or allocate from precomputed contiguous blocks per cabin. State the ordering rule unprompted.

items.title: Seat change after check-in?
items.text: Two-row atomic swap: lock both rows in sorted order, validate both, update both, bump seatmap version. Old seat must go AVAILABLE in the same transaction or you leak inventory.

items.title: How do you show a live seat map?
items.text: Versioned snapshot per flight (version++ on every confirm). Clients poll with If-None-Match; server pushes via websocket/SSE on version change. Reads never touch the primary.

items.title: Graceful overload at T-24h?
items.text: Per-flight token bucket on confirm QPS, Redis-hold first so DB only sees real intent, fast 429 with retry-after plus cached seatmap. Protect the primary, degrade UX honesty.

items.title: No-show, standby, and gate close?
items.text: Freeze confirms at gate-close timestamp; standby queue promotes in order via same confirm path. Un-check-in after close is rejected — say it, do not allow negative inventory.

items: Double-click / retry with same `Idempotency-Key` returns the original boarding pass, never a second seat.
Hold expires between pick and confirm — confirm must fail with `410 HoldExpired`, not silently steal another passenger's hold.
Two passengers, one PNR, same seat selected — second gets `409` inside the transaction.
Un-check-in of already-boarded passenger is rejected; `BOARDED` is terminal.
Flight swap / aircraft change invalidates all seatIds — version the layout, wipe holds, reassign by cabin, notify.
Orphan holds from crashed clients auto-expire via Redis TTL plus a sweeper that reconciles `HELD` rows older than TTL.
Clock skew on eligibility window — enforce window server-side on flight departure time, never client time.
Seat map version mismatch on confirm — client must refetch; never auto-downgrade to a random seat without consent.

blocks.title: 45-minute plan
blocks.text: 0-5 min: lock scope and state machine. 5-12 min: API + requirements table. 12-20 min: naive + why double-assign happens. 20-32 min: partitioned Postgres + Redis holds + confirm transaction code. 32-40 min: contention deep-dive (hot seat queue, group locking order, idempotency). 40-45 min: outbox, overload, and aircraft-swap edge cases. Close with: **fixed inventory means correctness first, speed second — serialize the seat, not the flight.**
